claim: The cerebellar BOLD signal does not reflect the activity levels of Purkinje cells, the output of the cerebellar cortex.
source: The cerebellar blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal does not reflect the activity levels of Purkinje cells, the output of the cerebellar cortex (Caesar et al., 2003a; Thomsen et al., 2004; Thomsen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caesar et al., 2003a; Thomsen et al., 2004; Thomsen et al., 2009

claim: The cerebellar BOLD signal is determined solely by mossy fiber and climbing fiber input.
source: Rather, it is determined solely by mossy fiber (Akgören et al., 1994; Gagliano et al., 2022; Mapelli et al., 2017) and climbing fiber (Caesar et al., 2003b; Mathiesen et al., 2000) input, with the former likely playing the dominant role (Attwell and Iadecola, 2002; Howarth et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on mossy fiber and climbing fiber contributions

claim: Mossy fibers carry input from a wide array of neocortical areas, including prefrontal and parietal association cortices.
source: Mossy fibers carry input from a wide array of neocortical areas, including prefrontal and parietal association cortices, as demonstrated directly through viral tracing studies in non-human primates (Kelly and Strick, 2003), and indirectly through resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) analysis in humans (Buckner et al., 2011; Ji et al., 2019; Marek et al., 2018; O'Reilly et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to viral tracing studies and resting-state functional connectivity analyses

claim: The best performing connectivity model could predict about 50% of the reliable variance in the cerebellar cortex across tasks.
source: Second, when given a cortical activation pattern, the best performing model could predict about 50% of the reliable variance in the cerebellar cortex across tasks (King et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to King et al., 2023

claim: Patients with cerebellar damage consistently show impairments in performing rapid alternating movements, a symptom called dysdiadochokinesia.
source: Patients with cerebellar damage consistently show impairments in performing rapid alternating movements, a symptom called dysdiadochokinesia (Hallett et al., 1991; Mai et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies

claim: Patients with cerebellar damage are generally able to exert grip forces comparable to healthy controls.
source: In contrast, these patients are generally able to exert grip forces comparable to healthy controls (Mai et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mai et al., 1988

claim: Cerebellar activation, particularly in Lobules VI, VII, and VIII is consistently observed in fMRI studies of working memory.
source: Cerebellar activation, particularly in Lobules VI, Crus I, and VIII is consistently observed in fMRI studies of working memory (Cohen et al., 1997; Courtney et al., 1997; D'Esposito and Postle, 2015; Nee et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple fMRI studies

claim: Patients with cerebellar damage tend to show deficits in verbal working memory tasks.
source: Furthermore, patients with cerebellar damage tend to show deficits in verbal working memory tasks (Cooper et al., 2012; Ilg et al., 2013; Kansal et al., 2017; Peterburs et al., 2010; Ravizza et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple patient studies

claim: Participants complied well with task instructions in the motor task, as evidenced by group-averaged peak forces and number of taps being close to target values.
source: Participants complied well with task instructions, as evidenced by the group-averaged peak forces and number of taps, which were close to the target values (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Table 1

claim: The combined M1/S1 region showed a significant activation increase in the high-force condition compared to baseline (t15 = 9.41, p = 1.10 × 10−7).
source: Compared to the baseline condition, the combined M1/S1 region of interest (ROI) showed a significant activation increase in the high-force (t15 = 9.41, p = 1.10 × 10−7) and the high-speed conditions (t15 = 8.29, p = 5.54 × 10−7).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: The combined M1/S1 region showed a significant activation increase in the high-speed condition compared to baseline (t15 = 8.29, p = 5.54 × 10−7).
source: Compared to the baseline condition, the combined M1/S1 region of interest (ROI) showed a significant activation increase in the high-force (t15 = 9.41, p = 1.10 × 10−7) and the high-speed conditions (t15 = 8.29, p = 5.54 × 10−7).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: Activity in the right anterior and posterior motor areas of the cerebellum increased with increasing force (t15 = 14.21, p = 4.14 × 10−10).
source: Similarly, activity in the right anterior and posterior motor areas of the cerebellum (outlined in light gray in Figure 2, see Methods for details on ROI) increased with increasing force (t15 = 14.21, p = 4.14 × 10−10) and speed (t15 = 7.60, p = 1.59 × 10−6).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: Activity in the right anterior and posterior motor areas of the cerebellum increased with increasing speed (t15 = 7.60, p = 1.59 × 10−6).
source: Similarly, activity in the right anterior and posterior motor areas of the cerebellum (outlined in light gray in Figure 2, see Methods for details on ROI) increased with increasing force (t15 = 14.21, p = 4.14 × 10−10) and speed (t15 = 7.60, p = 1.59 × 10−6).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: Increasing speed led to more widespread activation in secondary motor areas compared to increasing force.
source: However, the neocortical activation patterns for speed and force conditions were not completely matched (Figure 2A vs. 2C): Increasing speed led to more widespread activation in secondary motor areas compared to increasing force.
evidence: Supported by visual inspection of activation maps in Figure 2

claim: The predicted values from the connectivity model closely match the observed cerebellar values (average R2 = 0.60, standard error of the mean = 0.01).
source: In general, the predicted values closely match the observed values (average R2 = 0.60, standard error of the mean = 0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis comparing predicted and observed values

claim: There was a significant effect of condition on signed residuals (F4, 60 = 6.796, p = 1.1 × 10−4).
source: To test for systematic deviations across subjects, we submitted the signed residuals for all conditions to a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), revealing a significant effect of condition (F4, 60 = 6.796, p = 1.1 × 10−4).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA statistical test

claim: The signed residual for the high-speed condition was significantly higher than for the high-force condition (t15 = 2.37, p = 0.0157).
source: Post hoc tests revealed that the signed residual for the high-speed condition was significantly higher than for the high-force condition (t15 = 2.37, p = 0.0157).
evidence: Supported by post hoc statistical test

claim: The signed residual for medium speed was significantly higher than for medium force (t15 = 1.94, p = 0.035).
source: This was also the case when comparing medium speed and medium force (t15 = 1.94, p = 0.035).
evidence: Supported by post hoc statistical test

claim: The increases in cerebellar activity for speed outstripped the activity increases for force, even when accounting for differences in neocortical input regions.
source: In summary, the increases in cerebellar activity for speed outstripped the activity increases for force, even when we accounted for differences in activity for the two conditions in neocortical input regions.
evidence: Supported by analysis of residuals from connectivity model predictions

claim: Error rates in the working memory task increased with memory load.
source: As expected, error rates increased with memory load and were also higher in the backwards condition.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Error rates in the working memory task were higher in the backwards condition.
source: As expected, error rates increased with memory load and were also higher in the backwards condition.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The verbal working memory task led to high activity in the fronto-parietal network during the encoding and retrieval phases.
source: Consistent with previous imaging studies, the verbal working memory task led to high activity in the fronto-parietal network (Cohen et al., 1997; Courtney et al., 1997; D'Esposito and Postle, 2015; Nee et al., 2013; Owen et al., 2005) during the encoding and retrieval phases (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 5 and citations to previous studies

claim: During the retrieval phase, activation was observed in cortical motor areas, reflecting the response requirements of the task.
source: During the latter phase, we also observed activation in cortical motor areas, reflecting the response requirements of the task.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data and inference about task demands

claim: Within the cerebellum, encoding and retrieval activated a superior region (lateral parts of lobule VI, extending to Crus I), as well as an inferior region (VIIb and VIIIa).
source: Within the cerebellum, encoding and retrieval activated a superior region (lateral parts of lobule VI, extending to Crus I), as well as an inferior region (VIIb and VIIIa) (Chen and Desmond, 2005; Desmond et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data and citations to previous studies

claim: For verbal working memory, the activity was more pronounced in the right than in the left cerebellar hemisphere.
source: As observed previously for verbal working memory, the activity was more pronounced in the right than in the left cerebellar hemisphere (Desmond and Fiez, 1998).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data and citation to previous study

claim: The connectivity model predicted cerebellar activity relatively well at the individual level (R2 = 0.42, standard error = 0.01) for the working memory task.
source: After fitting a linear regression to account for scale differences between predicted and observed activations, we found that the predicted values matched the observed values relatively well at the individual level (R2 = 0.42, standard error = 0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of model predictions

claim: There was a systematic deviation of residuals across participants in the working memory task (F11, 165 = 2.22, p = 0.0156).
source: A repeated 1-factor measures ANOVA on the residuals across all 12 conditions found a systematic deviation across participants (F11, 165 = 2.22, p = 0.0156).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA statistical test

claim: There was a significant two-way interaction between load and phase in the working memory task (F2, 30 = 4.38, p = 0.02).
source: When we analyze the residuals using a 2 (phase) × 2 (recall direction) × 3 (load) ANOVA, we found a significant two-way interaction between load and phase (F2, 30 = 4.38, p = 0.02), but no significant effect of recall direction (F1, 15 = 0.95, p = 0.34).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA statistical test

claim: There was no significant effect of recall direction on residuals in the working memory task (F1, 15 = 0.95, p = 0.34).
source: When we analyze the residuals using a 2 (phase) × 2 (recall direction) × 3 (load) ANOVA, we found a significant two-way interaction between load and phase (F2, 30 = 4.38, p = 0.02), but no significant effect of recall direction (F1, 15 = 0.95, p = 0.34).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA statistical test

claim: The results indicate selective recruitment of the cerebellum when the number of items to be encoded into working memory is high.
source: Thus, the results indicate selective recruitment of the cerebellum when the number of items to be encoded into working memory is high, an effect that holds for both the forward and backwards conditions.
evidence: Supported by analysis of residuals showing greater-than-predicted activity during high-load encoding

claim: Increases in cerebellar BOLD signal could simply reflect the automatic transmission of neocortical activity through fixed anatomical connections.
source: This means that increases in the cerebellar BOLD signal could simply reflect the automatic transmission of neocortical activity through fixed anatomical connections.
evidence: Logical inference from the fact that cerebellar BOLD reflects mossy fiber input from neocortex

claim: Whenever a task activates a neocortical region, the corresponding cerebellar region would also be activated, regardless of whether the cerebellum is directly involved in the task or not.
source: As such, whenever a task activates a neocortical region, the corresponding cerebellar region would also be activated, regardless of whether the cerebellum is directly involved in the task or not.
evidence: Logical inference from fixed anatomical connectivity

claim: The fact that the prediction of connectivity models did not reach the theoretically possible prediction accuracy suggests that the connectivity between the neocortex and cerebellum may not be fully task-invariant.
source: The fact that the prediction of these models did not reach the theoretically possible prediction accuracy suggests that the connectivity between the neocortex and cerebellum may not be fully task-invariant.
evidence: Inference from model performance data

claim: Neocortical input to the cerebellum may be modulated as a function of the relative importance of cerebellar computation in a task-specific manner.
source: Instead, neocortical input to the cerebellum may be modulated as a function of the relative importance of cerebellar computation in a task-specific manner.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed to explain deviations from task-invariant connectivity model

claim: Task- or state-dependent gating would make evolutionary sense, given the substantial metabolic cost of granule cell activity.
source: Such task- or state-dependent gating would make evolutionary sense, given the substantial metabolic cost of granule cell activity (Attwell and Iadecola, 2002; Howarth et al., 2010).
evidence: Inference based on metabolic considerations and citations

claim: Based on the selective recruitment hypothesis, increases in cerebellar BOLD will be greater for increases in tapping speed compared to increases in finger force output, even when the neocortical activity is matched between conditions.
source: Based on the selective recruitment hypothesis, we predicted that increases in cerebellar BOLD will be greater for increases in tapping speed compared to increases in finger force output, even when the neocortical activity is matched between conditions.
evidence: A priori prediction based on the selective recruitment hypothesis

claim: Both manipulations (speed and force) are expected to produce an increase in the BOLD response in neocortical motor areas.
source: Both manipulations are expected to produce an increase in the BOLD response in neocortical motor areas (Diedrichsen et al., 2013; Thickbroom et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The task-invariant connectivity model predicts increased cerebellar activity with both increases in speed and force.
source: As such, our task-invariant connectivity model predicts increased cerebellar activity with both increases in speed and force (Spraker et al., 2012).
evidence: Prediction from connectivity model and citation

claim: Selective recruitment predicts that for equivalent activity levels in the neocortex, cerebellar activity should be higher in the speed than in the force condition.
source: Critically, selective recruitment predicts that for equivalent activity levels in the neocortex, cerebellar activity should be higher in the speed than in the force condition.
evidence: Prediction from selective recruitment hypothesis

claim: According to the connectivity model, inputs to cerebellar M3 do not only come from contralateral M1 and S1, but also from premotor and supplementary motor regions.
source: According to the model, inputs to cerebellar M3 do not only come from contralateral M1 and S1, but also from premotor and supplementary motor regions.
evidence: Inference from connectivity model weights shown in Figure 3A

claim: The predicted difference in the residual for the high-speed vs. high-force condition remained significant when using an L1-regularized model (t15 = 2.373, p = 0.0315).
source: For both connectivity models, the predicted difference in the residual for the high-speed vs. high-force condition remained significant (L1 regression: t15 = 2.373, p = 0.0315, Fusion model: t15 = 2.140, p = 0.0492).
evidence: Supported by statistical test using alternative connectivity model

claim: The predicted difference in the residual for the high-speed vs. high-force condition remained significant when using a Fusion model (t15 = 2.140, p = 0.0492).
source: For both connectivity models, the predicted difference in the residual for the high-speed vs. high-force condition remained significant (L1 regression: t15 = 2.373, p = 0.0315, Fusion model: t15 = 2.140, p = 0.0492).
evidence: Supported by statistical test using alternative connectivity model

claim: The results indicate selective recruitment of the cerebellum when the demands on finger coordination are increased relative to when the demands on force output are increased.
source: Thus, consistent across various connectivity models, the results indicate selective recruitment of the cerebellum when the demands on finger coordination are increased relative to when the demands on force output are increased.
evidence: Inference from consistent findings across multiple connectivity models

claim: The connectivity weights suggest converging input from area 55b, premotor eye field, area 6r, and supplementary and cingulate eye field to cerebellar D3R.
source: The connectivity weights from the model (Figure 6A) suggest converging input from area 55b (located at the inferior end of the middle frontal gyrus), premotor eye field, area 6r (anterior to the primary motor cortex), and supplementary and cingulate eye field (SCEF, dorsomedial frontal cortex; Glasser et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference from connectivity model weights shown in Figure 6A

claim: There was one clear deviation where the observed cerebellar activation was greater than predicted: During encoding in the highest load condition.
source: Turning to our test of selective recruitment, there was one clear deviation where the observed cerebellar activation was greater than predicted (Figure 6B): During encoding in the highest load condition.
evidence: Supported by visual inspection of Figure 6B and subsequent statistical analysis

claim: The cerebellum has a special role in encoding larger item sets into working memory.
source: This suggests that the cerebellum has a special role in encoding larger item sets into working memory.
evidence: Inference from the finding of selective recruitment during high-load encoding

claim: Clinical studies have shown that cerebellar pathology results in a marked impairment in the ability to produce fast alternating movements, but has little impact on maximal force generation.
source: However, clinical studies have shown that cerebellar pathology results in a marked impairment in the ability to produce fast alternating movements, but has little impact on maximal force generation (Mai et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to clinical study

claim: Some observed change in cerebellar activity may not be functionally involved in controlling behavior.
source: This suggests that some observed change in cerebellar activity may not be functionally involved in controlling behavior.
evidence: Inference from the discrepancy between activation patterns and clinical findings

claim: A large proportion of the observed variation of cerebellar activity across tasks can be accounted for by fixed functional connections between neocortical and cerebellar regions.
source: As shown in our previous study (King et al., 2023), this model provides a good prediction of cerebellar activity across a broad range of tasks, including those not used in developing the model. This confirms that a large proportion of the observed variation of cerebellar activity across tasks can be accounted for by fixed functional connections between neocortical and cerebellar regions.
evidence: Supported by citation to King et al., 2023 study

claim: Systematic deviations from the null model would occur if neocortical input was upregulated when the cerebellum is required for a task.
source: The central idea explored in the current paper is that systematic deviations from this null model would occur, if neocortical input was upregulated when the cerebellum is required for a task (and/or downregulated when it is not).
evidence: Hypothesis proposed in the study

claim: If input to the cerebellum is gated in a task-specific manner, then it should be upregulated during the production of fast alternating finger movements as compared to the production of high forces with the same fingers.
source: If input to the cerebellum is gated in a task-specific manner, then it should be upregulated during the production of fast alternating finger movements as compared to the production of high forces with the same fingers.
evidence: A priori prediction based on selective recruitment hypothesis

claim: Activity in the cerebellar hand area increased more for increasing speed than force, even when activity in the neocortical hand areas was approximately matched across conditions.
source: This was indeed the case; activity in the cerebellar hand area increased more for increasing speed than force, even when activity in the neocortical hand areas was approximately matched across conditions.
evidence: Supported by analysis of fMRI data and connectivity model residuals

claim: These results provide clear evidence for task-dependent gating.
source: These results provide clear evidence for task-dependent gating (Cole et al., 2021).
evidence: Inference from the finding of differential cerebellar activation beyond predicted levels

claim: If the input to the cerebellum is upregulated in a task-specific manner, then the observed cerebellar activity should be larger than predicted using the simultaneously observed neocortical activity and a task-invariant connectivity model.
source: If the input to the cerebellum is upregulated in a task-specific manner, then the observed cerebellar activity should be larger than precited using the simultaneously observed neocortical activity and a task-invariant connectivity model.
evidence: Logical inference defining the operational criterion for selective recruitment

claim: Previous studies have consistently shown deficits in verbal working memory in cerebellar patients.
source: Previous studies have consistently shown deficits in verbal working memory in cerebellar patients (Ilg et al., 2013; Kansal et al., 2017; Ravizza et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to patient studies

claim: The exact nature of working memory deficits in cerebellar patients is still a matter of considerable debate.
source: The exact nature of these deficits, however, is still a matter of considerable debate.
evidence: Inference from variability in reported deficits in the literature

claim: The cerebellum is not necessary for a task when selective recruitment is not observed.
source: Finally, our approach does not allow us to conclude that the cerebellum is not necessary for a task when selective recruitment is not observed.
evidence: Explicit statement about limitations of the approach

claim: Much of cerebellar activity can be fully accounted for by a task-invariant transmission of information from the neocortex.
source: Our approach simply shows that much of cerebellar activity can be fully accounted for by a task-invariant transmission of information from the neocortex, raising the possibility that this observed activity is an epiphenomenon of cortical input.
evidence: Inference from connectivity model performance

claim: We should expect some cerebellar activity even when the cerebellum makes minimal contributions to task performance.
source: Given this, we should expect some cerebellar activity even when the cerebellum makes minimal contributions to task performance (as observed in the force condition).
evidence: Inference from the nature of fixed anatomical connectivity

claim: Showing task-specific violations on a task-invariant connectivity model provides much stronger evidence for a specific cerebellar role in a task than the mere presence of activity.
source: Overall, we believe that showing task-specific violations on a task-invariant connectivity model provides much stronger evidence for a specific cerebellar role in a task than the mere presence of activity.
evidence: Inference about the methodological advantage of the approach

claim: One obvious candidate for gating are the pontine nuclei which integrate descending signals from different neocortical areas with feedback signals from the cerebellum.
source: One obvious candidate for gating are the pontine nuclei which integrate descending signals from different neocortical areas with feedback signals from the cerebellum (Schwarz and Thier, 1999).
evidence: Speculation based on known anatomy and citation

claim: The cellular properties of pontine neurons are ideal for gating input signals in a state-dependent manner.
source: The cellular properties of pontine neurons are ideal for gating input signals in a state-dependent manner (Möck et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on pontine neuron properties

claim: Gating could be achieved via modulation within the granule cell layer itself, perhaps via recurrent loops involving inhibitory Golgi cells.
source: Alternatively, gating could be achieved via modulation within the granule cell layer itself, perhaps via recurrent loops involving inhibitory Golgi cells (Maex and De Schutter, 1998).
evidence: Speculation based on cerebellar circuitry and citation

claim: Violations of the connectivity model may also be caused by increased climbing fiber input under specific task conditions.
source: Violations of our connectivity model may also be caused by increased climbing fiber input under specific task conditions.
evidence: Speculation about alternative mechanism

claim: Gating may already occur in the neocortex, with more recruitment of neocortical neurons that project to the pons when controlling the spatial aspects of joystick manipulation.
source: Finally, gating may already occur in the neocortex: A recent study (Park et al., 2022) showed more recruitment of neocortical neurons that project to the pons when controlling the spatial aspects of joystick manipulation, and more recruitment of neurons that project intra-cortically or to the striatum when controlling movement amplitude.
evidence: Speculation based on citation to recent study

claim: Pontine-projecting neurons may be more engaged during fast alternating movements, even though the fMRI activity is the same as during the production of high forces.
source: Because the neocortical BOLD signal reflects the activity of both neuronal populations, pontine-projecting neurons may be more engaged during fast alternating movements, even though the fMRI activity is the same as during the production of high forces.
evidence: Speculation about differential engagement of neuronal populations

claim: Task-dependent gating of inputs to the cerebellum would be highly adaptive from a metabolic standpoint.
source: Whichever combination of mechanisms is responsible for our observed effect, task-dependent gating of inputs to the cerebellum would be highly adaptive from a metabolic standpoint (Attwell and Iadecola, 2002): the costly mossy-fiber system would be most activated when cerebellar computation is required.
evidence: Inference based on metabolic considerations and citation

claim: Task-dependent gating offers a promising new approach that may allow researchers to use fMRI for testing cerebellar contributions across cognitive tasks.
source: For us as researchers, this gating phenomena offers a promising new keyhole that may allow us to unlock the use of fMRI for testing cerebellar contributions across cognitive tasks (Diedrichsen et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference about the methodological implications of the findings

claim: A total of 21 participants started the experiment.
source: A total of 21 participants started the experiment.
evidence: Direct statement of participant numbers

claim: Four participants were not scanned because of poor performance during the behavioral training session.
source: Of these, four participants were not scanned because of poor performance during the behavioral training session.
evidence: Direct statement about participant exclusion

claim: The data for one participant were excluded due to an incidental finding.
source: The data for one participant were excluded due to an incidental finding.
evidence: Direct statement about data exclusion

claim: The analyses were based on the data from 16 participants (8 females, 8 males, mean age = 25, std age = 2).
source: Therefore, the analyses were based on the data from 16 participants (8 females, 8 males, mean age = 25, std age = 2).
evidence: Direct statement of final sample characteristics

claim: MRI data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Prisma at the Center for Functional and Metabolic Mapping (CFMM) at Western University.
source: MRI data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Prisma at the Center for Functional and Metabolic Mapping (CFMM) at Western University.
evidence: Direct statement of data acquisition details

claim: Whole-brain functional images were acquired using an echo-planar imaging sequence with TR = 1000 ms, TE = 30 ms, voxel size = 2.5 × 2.5 × 3 mm3.
source: Whole-brain functional images were acquired using an echo-planar imaging sequence with Repetition time (TR) = 1000 ms, Echo time (TE) = 30 ms, voxel size = 2.5 × 2.5 × 3 mm3, field-of-view = 20.8 × 20.8 × 20.8 cm3, 48 slices, P to A phase encoding direction, with multi-band acceleration factor = 3 (interleaved) and in-plane acceleration factor = 2.
evidence: Direct statement of imaging parameters
